lines: NASA lit it on purpose, inside an empty cargo spaceship, high above the Earth.
Because one day, people will live on the Moon... and up there, fire won't behave the way it does here.
On Earth, a flame stands tall: hot air rises, and pulls fresh air in behind it.
Take gravity away, and nothing rises.
The flame turns small, round, and blue... and lives or dies on the air drifting past it.
NASA has studied this for decades, but the answers are buried in technical reports.
MicroFire Atlas brings them to life: an adventure for young explorers, and a workstation for mission planners.
Explorers start by flipping gravity off,
then building NASA's real wind tunnel, piece by piece.
Next, a real NASA flame. The computer traces it, frame by frame, and measures it in pixels.
Then a puzzle: turn the airflow down on test B20.
The atlas finds the real test, but hides the answer. Predict first!
Then NASA's own words appear, with the exact page they came from.
Next stop: the Moon. Sort real clues onto the Evidence Ladder.
Tiny burning droplets? They explain how fire works. Not how plastic burns.
And the top rung stays empty. No record in this atlas matches these conditions yet.
Every page has a quest, and every real discovery lights a star.
In the Atlas, you become a data detective. Find the lowest oxygen where a flame kept burning... Solved!
And meet LUCI: fires in Moon-like gravity, made by a spinning rocket.
The biggest fires? NASA lit them inside empty cargo spaceships: the Saffire experiments.
Twenty runs, and every number traced to its line in a NASA table.
Mission planners pick a NASA cabin atmosphere. Every tick underneath is a real NASA test.
Slide to thirty-four percent oxygen... and you're in empty space.
So MicroFire says it plainly: the evidence doesn't cover this yet. No risk score. No guessing.
Then it ranks NASA's own findings, and explains why each one matters, and where it doesn't.
Can you trust it? Every ranking is re-run a thousand ways,
and the AI is graded on a hundred test questions.
Try to fool the claim checker. Made-up numbers, fake citations, Moon claims from orbit tests... it catches them.
And when NASA finally burns materials on the Moon itself, in its FM-two experiment,
MicroFire already shows which open questions it's built to answer.
Real NASA data. A real adventure. And honest answers about what we still don't know.
